newsitem.title: SPAIN: Analysts say Spain budget opens way for rate cut.
newsitem.headline: Analysts say Spain budget opens way for rate cut.

text.p: The Spanish government's draft budget for 1997 offered few surprises and left the way clear for the Bank of Spain to cut rates by up to 50 basis points, analysts said on Friday.
"It was pretty much as expected," said Adrian Schmidt, international economist at Chase Manhattan in London. "A rate cut is in the market, it's almost a formality by now."

The Bank of Spain is expected to cut its key money market rate by at least a quarter-point from 7.25 percent at its regular repurchase tender on Thursday, after the government formally presents the budget to parliament on Monday.
But economists say that has already been discounted and markets are now starting to look for a half-point cut.
"(Economy Minister Rodrigo) Rato said what we hoped he would say, he didn't surprise us," said Alfredo Urrutia, capital markets economist at Societe Generale in Madrid.

"The market liked the fact that he said the numbers he was supposed to say," he added. "A cut of 25 basis points is already discounted, now we can see even 50 basis points because of the strength of the peseta."
Traders suspect the Bank of Spain has intervened several times this week to brake the peseta's rise against the mark.
They thought the Spanish central bank was selling pesetas at 84.09 against the mark on Friday morning, having intervened at 84.05 earlier in the week.

Rato said the government, which approved the draft budget at a cabinet meeting earlier, foresaw spending would rise 1.7 percent in 1997, revenues would increase nearly six percent and the budget deficit would fall to three percent of GDP.
Analysts agreed the forecasts were in line with what markets were expecting with only a few expressing reservations.
"It's not a bad budget," said one analyst, adding: "The growth and inflation forecasts are slightly optimistic."
The government maintained its forecast that gross domestic product will grow by three percent in 1997 while inflation will be brought down to 2.7 percent.
The Spanish economy grew 1.9 percent in the second quarter of 1996, according to figures released earlier this week, and the official target is 2.3 percent growth by year-end.

Analysts say that even if Spain fails to meet the criteria needed to join a single European currency in 1999, it will come close and its efforts will allow it to join a European economic and monetary union (EMU) in a second membership phase.
